title: Infra playbook: GPU fleet, capacity, cloud accounts, IaC modules, and CI/CD (consolidated)
author: Aisha Khatri
body:
Overview

This consolidated playbook describes Redwood's recommended patterns and runbooks for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD for inference infrastructure. It is intended for infra engineers, platform owners, SREs, and solutions engineers working on Dedicated and Private deployments.

Scope

- GPU fleet sizing and autoscaling guidelines for hosted and dedicated pools
- Account and VPC design patterns for multi-tenant and single-tenant customers
- Terraform module standards and module registry practices
- CI/CD pipeline patterns for infra changes and model-serving releases
- Day-2 runbooks: incident response, scale-up, rollback, upgrade, and emergency procedures

Goals

1. Keep single-request P90 latency targets for hosted low-latency routes <= 250ms per-token server-side (where feasible).
2. Maintain cost-per-token guardrails via batching/quantization knobs in Redwood Optimize.
3. Provide repeatable IaC modules and safe CI/CD practices with automated policy checks.
4. Shorten mean time to scale (MTTS) for fleet expansions to < 2 hours for planned capacity increases.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: infra/gpu-capacity (team lead: Daniel Park)
- Secondary owner (networking & accounts): infra/cloudops (lead: Maya Ortega)
- Oncall escalation: infra-oncall -> platform-sre -> eng-infra lead (see Oncall and Escalation section)

Capacity planning process (quarterly + burst)

1. Forecast inputs: historical qps, percentiles (P50/P90/P99), model mix, expected growth (%), and enterprise commit contracts.
2. Compute baseline GPU-hours using per-model throughput profiles (see Appendix table). Use utilization target: 65% sustained for Dedicated; 55% for Hosted pools.
3. Reserve buffer: +20% planned capacity for scheduled growth, +30% for enterprise onboarding windows.
4. Approval workflow: submit capacity request via infra capacity tracker (Jira project INFRA-CAP), include cost estimate and region placement.
5. Procurement and scheduling: cloud account owner schedules quota increases and reserve instances as needed.

Autoscaling patterns and knobs

- Pod-based pools (k8s): use a hybrid horizontal/vertical scaler with the following parameters:
  - scale_up_threshold: 0.75 (avg GPU util across pool)
  - scale_down_threshold: 0.35
  - scale_cooldown: 300s
  - min_replicas: region-specific, default 2
  - max_replicas: tied to committed capacity and budget alerts
- Placement policy: prefer AZ-balanced placement; fallback to burst region policy when local AZs exceed 85% capacity.
- Warm pools: maintain a warm pool of pre-initialized containers for the top 3 models to reduce cold-starts (target < 500ms cold-start).

Terraform / IaC module standards

Principles:
- Modules must be composable, idempotent, and documented.
- Input/output variables must be explicit and typed. Avoid implicit magic variables.
- Keep provider usage isolated: network modules do not create compute, compute modules require a network_id variable.
- Version pinning: module registry versions must be semver (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).

Required module docs (each module in registry must include):
- README.md with overview, example usage, inputs, outputs, and permissions required
- acceptance_tests/ which include simple terraform apply -> destroy integration test
- CHANGELOG.md following keep-a-changelog format

Module review checklist (CI gate):
1. Linting (terraform fmt && tflint) passes
2. Unit tests for helper functions (if any) pass
3. Acceptance test smoke run in ephemeral account succeeds
4. Security scan (checkov/terrascan) reports no high/critical findings
5. Module pinned version bump where applicable

Sample module table (Appendix)

| Module name | Purpose | Inputs (key) | Outputs (key) | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| redwood/vpc | VPC & subnets | cidr_block, azs | vpc_id, subnet_ids | infra/cloudops |
| redwood/gpu-pool | GPU autoscaling pool | instance_type, gpu_count, network_id | pool_id, instance_ids | infra/gpu-capacity |
| redwood/iam-roles | Service roles and policies | principals | role_arn | infra/security |

Cloud accounts and networking patterns

Account topology:
- Org root (billing) -> management account -> workload accounts by environment (prod-hosted, prod-dedicated, staging, dev, partner-onprem).
- Dedicated/Private customer accounts: created per-customer for strong isolation where contract requires.

VPC and subnet strategy:
- Use three-tier subnets: public (LB), private (services), restricted (KMS/HSM/data-plane)
- Network ACLs: default deny on restricted subnets.
- Transit architecture: use Transit Gateway for multi-account routing; tag routes with cost-center and team for billing.

Connectivity patterns for Private deployments:
- Support VPC peering and Transit Gateway-based connectivity. For on-prem, provide a Site-to-Site VPN blueprint and optional Direct Connect.
- KMS integration: customer-managed CMKs supported; store key metadata in account registry (encrypted).

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline types:
- Module CI: runs on module registry PRs; gates: fmt, tflint, unit tests, acceptance smoke, security scans, semantic-release.
- Infra deployment pipeline: staged promotion across accounts (dev -> staging -> prod) using pipeline-as-code.
- Runtime release pipeline: model-serving runtime changes require canary deploys and automated perf regression tests.

Pipeline safeguards:
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Conftest) enforces network and iam constraints before apply.
- Manual approvals for prod apply for changes that touch capacity, networking, or IAM.
- Canary window: 30 minutes with traffic mirroring 5-10% for runtime changes.

Sample CI configuration snippets (example):
- Terraform module PR job: terraform fmt && tflint && terraform init -backend=false && run acceptance smoke test.
- Deployment job: terraform plan -> upload plan artifact -> require manual approve -> terraform apply using ephemeral assume-role creds.

Runbooks and operational procedures

High-level runbooks (short links in registry):
1. Scale Up GPU Pool (planned)
   - Owner: infra/gpu-capacity
   - Steps: Update tfvars with desired replica count -> run plan -> get approval -> apply -> verify pool health & infra metrics -> update capacity tracker.
2. Emergency scale-up (unplanned burst)
   - Owner: oncall SRE
   - Steps: Temporary policy: allow burst scale to emergency pool (pre-approved IAM role) -> trigger warm pool bootstrapping job -> notify capacity lead -> open incident ticket and set severity.
3. Rollback runtime release
   - Owner: runtime release lead
   - Steps: Abort rollout -> revert to previous runtime image (immutable tags) -> validate regression tests -> mark release as failed and create postmortem if SLA breach.
4. Network/Account outage (Transit Gateway)
   - Owner: infra/cloudops
   - Steps: Validate TGW health -> check route table associations and TGW attachments -> failover to secondary peering where configured -> initiate provider support ticket if hardware/region issue.

Monitoring and SLOs

- Telemetry: GPU utilization, queue length, P95 token latency per-route, infra errors, model error rate.
- SLOs: P95 per-token latency <= 450ms for background batch routes; P95 <= 250ms for low-latency hosted routes.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - GPU utilization sustained > 85% for 10m -> warn (capacity planning)
  - Queue length > 1000 pending requests -> page oncall SRE
  - Failed terraform apply > 3 in 1h -> page infra owner

Change windows and upgrade strategy

- Major infra upgrades: schedule in off-peak windows (weekend nights local region) with runbook and rollback playbook prepared.
- Rolling kernel/driver upgrades on GPU nodes: drain nodes one AZ at a time, validate KV-cache behavior, maintain global traffic routing to healthy AZs.

Oncall and escalation

- First responder: infra-oncall (primary), follow runbook relevant to symptom.
- Escalation path: infra-oncall -> infra lead -> platform-sre -> eng-infra director.
- Pager rotations and runbook links are maintained in the oncall roster (internal Confluence roster page).

Post-incident and reliability initiatives

- Postmortem templates: provide timeline, impact, root cause, corrective actions. All P1/P2 incidents must have a postmortem within 72 hours.
- Reliability initiatives: targeted efforts (three-month cycles) for reducing cold-starts, lowering tail latency, and reducing unit GPU-hour cost by 10% year-over-year.

Appendix: example terraform workflow (commands)

1. Local development:
   - git checkout -b feature/iam-fix
   - terraform init -backend=false
   - terraform fmt && tflint
   - terraform validate
2. Module PR CI executes acceptance smoke test in ephemeral account
3. Promotion:
   - terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -out=plans/prod.plan
   - upload plan artifact; obtain approval
   - terraform apply "plans/prod.plan"

Appendix: per-model throughput quick reference (example numbers)

- model-16k-8b: 25 tokens/sec per-GPU (fp16)
- model-8k-3b: 60 tokens/sec per-GPU (fp16)
- llama-7b-quant: 45 tokens/sec per-GPU (int8)

References and related docs

- infra-gpu-fleet-capacity-and-iac-ci-cd-playbook-2026 (linked)
- infra-iac-modules-ci-cd-guidelines-2026
- infra-gpu-capacity-and-iac-runbook-2026

Document maintenance

- Review cadence: quarterly; owners must review and update after any major incident or capacity change.
- Contact the owners above to request changes or submit a PR to the module registry and this page via the documentation repo.
summary: Consolidated engineering playbook covering GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform modules, CI/CD, and operational runbooks for Redwood Inference.
